title: Looking back: the code

lines: A STRIP OF BARE DIRT ACROSS THE GRASS.
cards: Across a park lawn runs a strip of bare dirt where the grass gave up. Planners call it a desire line. Nobody drew it on a map.

Feet made it, one person after another choosing the same way, until the way was visible. A way of life can grow like that. It can also be written down, so the next person doesn't have to guess where the path runs.
This year the path walked through one written way, the Sikh Rehat Maryada, a section at a time. Today, a look back at the whole, and why it's fair to call it a way.

teach.b: First, the code's shape. After it answers who a Sikh is, it sorts Sikh living into two sides: a Sikh's personal life, and the life of the panth, the community together. This year's sections hang on one side or the other.

In paraphrase, the code names three things: meditating on the Name and the scriptures, living by the Gurus' teaching, and serving others. Not first a journey or a uniform: ordinary things, kept every day.

The panth side holds the shared shape: the sangat and the gurdwara, the langar, the amrit and the Khalsa's discipline, and the ways the community settles questions together. Third, why the two sides belong together.

teach.h: GURU RAM DAS: A SIKH'S DAY.
teach.b: The code's daily pattern leans on a passage by Guru Ram Das, met early in that block.
In paraphrase: whoever calls themselves a Sikh of the true Guru rises early and remembers the Name, and keeps the Guru's word through the day.
Then the passage turns: Nanak asks for the dust of the feet of the Sikh who remembers the Name and helps others remember it too. One person's morning, then the turn toward others.
A code makes that pattern specific enough to share, so strangers can walk it side by side. Fourth, nobody walks a whole path at once.
The booklet holds a lifetime, but a day is kept one practice at a time: a morning prayer, a covered head, a shared meal, an hour of seva.
Step by step, the page becomes a path, worn in by the people who walk it.

how: Sikhs look to the Sikh Rehat Maryada for a shared pattern of personal practice, such as the daily prayers, Naam and seva, and of congregational life in the gurdwara, the langar and the amrit.

o: a ban on changing any custom handed down
a rite for asking pardon for the past year's wrongs
a year-end look at the Sikh code as one shared way

games.q: what's inside the code: tap the pairs.
p: rises early and remembers the Name

s: the code is only about one person's private habits
it sorts Sikh living into two sides: personal life and the life of the panth together.
Guru Ram Das's picture of a Sikh's day ends by turning toward others
it ends with Nanak asking for the dust of the feet of the Sikh who remembers the Name and helps others remember it too.
the personal side of the code begins with a pilgrimage
it begins with meditating on the Name and the scriptures, then the Gurus' teaching, then service.

games.q: you've read the code and want to begin. where does its list for a Sikh's personal life start?
o: with meditating on the Name and the scriptures.
with a journey to a Takht.
games.why: the Name and the scriptures come first, then living by the Gurus' teaching, then serving others. ordinary things, kept every day.

practice: Choose one of the code's three and stay with it: the Name, repeating Waheguru with each breath if you like; the Gurus' teaching, one line of theirs from this year; or service, one person you could serve and the first small step.
If your mind wanders, come back to the same one. If you pray, this can be your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Looking back. Today, at the code: a written way, with a personal side and a panth side, kept one practice at a time. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: rehat, the Sikh way of living, as in Rehat Maryada, the code.

carryVoice: Your line: the way. A written way, kept by walking it. That's today's step, done.

sources.ref: Sikh Rehat Maryada: the division of Sikh living into personal life and Panthic life; personal life as meditation on Naam and the scriptures, living by the Gurus' teachings, and altruistic service
